# Wikipedia: A Short Research Summary

**What it is.** Wikipedia is a free, web-based, collaborative, multilingual encyclopedia written and maintained by a community of volunteer editors using wiki software. It is the largest and most-read reference work in history, operated by the nonprofit Wikimedia Foundation and released under a free license (CC BY-SA) [1][2].

**Founding.** It was launched on **January 15, 2001** by **Jimmy Wales** and **Larry Sanger** as an offshoot of Nupedia, an earlier expert-written encyclopedia project. Sanger proposed the wiki model and coined the name "Wikipedia"; both men are generally credited as co-founders, despite a long-running dispute over Sanger's role [1][2][3].

**How it works.** Most pages can be edited by anyone, with every change recorded in a permanent revision history. Content is governed by core policies — Neutral Point of View, Verifiability, and No Original Research — summarized in the "Five Pillars" [1]. Roughly a quarter-million active volunteer editors (5+ edits/month) produce all content, organized through a meritocratic ladder of user rights up to ~1,000 English-Wikipedia administrators and an Arbitration Committee, the final internal dispute-resolution body [4][5]. The Wikimedia Foundation (founded 2003, ~$180M annual revenue) owns the servers and software but does **not** control editorial content, which rests with the volunteer community operating by consensus [4][6]. Automation (2,000+ approved bots such as ClueBot NG) helps revert vandalism within seconds [4].

**Size.** As of 2025, the English edition holds roughly **7 million articles**; all ~330 language editions combined contain about **64 million articles**, though depth varies enormously by language [7][8].

**Reliability and citations.** The landmark 2005 *Nature* study found Wikipedia's science articles roughly comparable in accuracy to Encyclopædia Britannica (~4 vs. ~3 errors per article) [9]. However, quality varies by topic and language edition — e.g., a 2014 study found 9 of 10 articles on the costliest medical conditions contained claims conflicting with peer-reviewed literature [10]. Wikipedia's Verifiability policy requires claims to be backed by reliable published sources; the site contains 20+ million citations, but these skew toward news and general web sources over scholarship, and link rot (at times ~30% of cited links dead) remains a persistent problem [11][12]. Academically, Wikipedia is regarded as a tertiary source and starting point, not a citable authority [10].

---

### Sources
